greek: Κατῴκει δὲ Ιακωβ ἐν τῇ γῇ, οὗ παρῴκησεν ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ, ἐν γῇ Χανααν.
hint: Jacob settles in the land where his father had lived as a sojourner.

notes.text: κατοικέω, to settle in, against παροικέω, to dwell beside: the one who settles and the one who lived alongside as a resident alien. The imperfect κατῴκει is a continuing state.
The Hebrew has a noun phrase, the land of his father's sojournings (mĕgûrê ʾābîw); the Greek makes it a clause with a verb, where his father dwelt beside.

hint: The heading of the next section, the line of Jacob, which opens on Joseph at seventeen and the report he brought against his brothers.

notes.text: The section formula of 25:12, 25:19 and 36:1. What follows is chiefly about Joseph, but the heading names Jacob.
Printed as two words, ten and seven, each a numeral in the genitive of age; read as two words here, as the morphology has them.
εἰμί with a present participle: was, and kept on being, shepherding — a continuing occupation, not one act.
ψόγος is blame or a fault found; anarthrous, so a report of fault, with nothing in the Greek to say whose fault it was.
The Hebrew has to their father; the Greek names him, to Israel their father.

hint: Jacob's love for Joseph above his other sons, and the tunic he made him.

notes.text: Imperfect of ἀγαπάω: a love that went on, not one act.

χιτών is the garment worn next to the skin; ποικίλος is many-coloured, spotted, or wrought in various colours. The Hebrew kĕtōnet passîm is of uncertain sense, perhaps a garment reaching to the extremities; the Greek reads it for colour or work.

greek: καὶ παρεπορεύοντο οἱ ἄνθρωποι οἱ Μαδιηναῖοι οἱ ἔμποροι, καὶ ἐξείλκυσαν καὶ ἀνεβίβασαν τὸν Ιωσηφ ἐκ τοῦ λάκκου καὶ ἀπέδοντο τὸν Ιωσηφ τοῖς Ισμαηλίταις εἴκοσι χρυσῶν, καὶ κατήγαγον τὸν Ιωσηφ εἰς Αἴγυπτον.
hint: Midianite merchants pass; Joseph is drawn up out of the pit, sold for twenty gold pieces, and taken to Egypt.

notes.text: The verbs that follow have no subject of their own. The nearest plural is the Midianite merchants; the brothers were the subject of 27. Either reading takes the grammar as it stands; the Greek does not name the subject.
Twenty of gold, χρυσοῦς used as a noun, gold pieces. The Hebrew has bĕʿeśrîm kāsep, for twenty of silver.
The Ishmaelites of 25 and 27 and the Midianites of this verse stand in one sentence as buyers and passers-by; the Hebrew has both peoples as well.

greek: οἱ δὲ Μαδιηναῖοι ἀπέδοντο τὸν Ιωσηφ εἰς Αἴγυπτον τῷ Πετεφρη τῷ σπάδοντι Φαραω, ἀρχιμαγείρῳ.
hint: The Midianites sell Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh's eunuch, the chief cook.

notes.text: The Hebrew has the Mĕdānîm here, a different spelling from the Midyānîm of 28; the Greek has Μαδιηναῖοι both times.
σπάδων, a eunuch, the plain sense of the word. The Hebrew sārîs can mean an officer as well as a eunuch.
ἀρχιμάγειρος, chief cook, one sense in LSJ, which adds that it is the title of a great officer in Oriental courts. The Hebrew has śar haṭṭabbāḥîm, chief of the slaughterers or guards.
